description: We are a crew of passionate engineers, systems programmers, and multi-hackathon winners driven by a shared love for space exploration and STEM. Armed with advanced expertise in SI, machine learning, and full-stack development, we bring a proven track record of rapidly building robust, high-impact solutions under tight pressure.
summary:
An experiment on the same material is not necessarily evidence for the same spacecraft environment. EMBER makes that difference visible.

For PMMA, BASS-50-69 records 22.4% oxygen at 100.1 kPa in microgravity. Our hypothetical lunar-rover scenario uses 30% at 70.3 kPa and lunar gravity. EMBER exposes each difference and links the comparison to the source table.

This interactive, SI-assisted dashboard summarizes findings, ranks relevant experiments and interprets conditions across 15 NASA PSI investigations with experimental test tables and 1,678 normalized records. In our 261-record solid-material flight subset with reported oxygen, the highest value is about 22.7%—a corpus coverage boundary, not a flammability threshold.

AI-assisted extraction and live, source-grounded answers to users’ research questions make the literature accessible; nine explicit applicability rules preserve experimental context. Researchers can inspect nearby tests and identify missing evidence without receiving an invented fire-risk percentage or a material-safety verdict. The dashboard also connects users to NASA-documented Earth applications in smoke detection and firefighter equipment.
details:
Why matching the material is not enough

“I am studying PMMA for a pressurized lunar rover. Which existing combustion tests address my conditions?” A paper about PMMA may describe a different atmosphere, gravity, specimen geometry or extinguishment method. EMBER turns those differences into an inspectable comparison.

In Mission lens, select the hypothetical lunar-rover scenario and PMMA, then choose Check historical evidence. The scenario uses 30% oxygen, 70.3 kPa and 0.166 g; these are comparison assumptions, not an established NASA rover specification. The deployed application reports no matching flight test in its indexed PSI corpus.

It then shows nearby records. BASS-50-69 used 22.4% oxygen, 100.1 kPa and microgravity. That leaves differences of 7.6 percentage points in oxygen, 29.8 kPa in pressure, and microgravity versus lunar gravity. The test is identified in the BASS experimental-table CSV, row 52; atmospheric values come from the As Run_Test Matrix workbook, worksheet “as run matrix”, row 54. The research-gap panel identifies the conditions still needing evidence.

From NASA records to useful comparisons

Our pipeline combines 15 NASA PSI investigations, 1,678 normalized records, 145 extracted claims with source quotations, and 68 source entries. It retains investigation links and source-table locations. The evidence map displays indexed conditions alongside mission scenarios; unknown dimensions are not plotted as zero. Investigation cards summarize objectives, fuels, apparatus and findings. CSV and JSON exports support further analysis and preparation of modeling datasets.

Among the 261 indexed solid-material flight records with reported oxygen, the highest reported value is approximately 22.7%. EMBER makes the distance between that coverage and the hypothetical rover scenario visible, while keeping later research outside the indexed PSI tables in view.

Interpretation preserves experimental context

Nine explicit applicability rules examine outcomes, material, geometry, unknown values, oxygen’s role in the apparatus, provenance, gravity, protocol and jointly tested conditions. Separate oxygen, pressure and airflow ranges cannot establish a jointly tested operating point. A high-oxygen gas-burner stream is not automatically evidence for a solid material in cabin air.

Protocol comparisons distinguish smoke measurements from flame spread and natural extinction from commanded suppression. For example, a nearby BASS record ended after the crew switched airflow off; that intervention is not a measured natural extinction limit. Users can follow the interpretation back to its recorded conditions and source.

Who benefits and why this addresses the challenge

EMBER serves aerospace engineers and researchers reviewing evidence for habitable crew environments, with the same source trail available to students. It connects the challenge’s three operations: summaries explain what was studied; rankings identify relevant records; interpretation explains what those records can support. Prevention, detection and suppression investigations retain their respective experimental contexts.

The intended benefit is better preparation for engineering review: find useful tests, expose assumptions before extrapolation and identify missing coverage. The Earth-applications section connects users to NASA-documented smoke detection, suppression and protective-equipment technologies.

Implementation, scope and validation

The working application combines a TypeScript scientific core, React/Vite interface, Python data pipeline and Three.js/WebGL visualization (source code available at https://github.com/itsamirkhon/EMBER). The Trust page documents development checks, baseline comparisons and known limitations. Its current backtest is exploratory, not established predictive accuracy; applicability tolerances and complex comparisons still require independent domain-expert review and a held-out evaluation.

Record counts include published summaries and reconstructed protocols, not 1,678 independent experiments. Planned conditions remain distinct from observations. Source-quote matching establishes that a quotation is present, not that every extracted interpretation is correct. The 22.7% boundary describes the indexed PSI subset, not all NASA research; later Saffire work and partial-gravity studies outside PSI also matter. Similarity scores are organizational heuristics, not calibrated probabilities. EMBER is an evidence-review tool: it does not calculate new flammability limits, simulate cabin combustion or certify spacecraft safety. Its procedural flame illustration is educational.

Additional NASA background references

The NASA Data field lists the experimental investigations, Earth applications and challenge resources. Further background and supporting reports:

  • PSI Data Repository: Combustion Science — NASA experimental data discovery
  • NASA ScienceCasts: The Power of Studying Combustion on the ISS — educational introduction, not quantitative test data
  • Apollo 1 — historical context
  • Apollo 13 — historical context
  • 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir — historical context

Flame in Freefall: official challenge resources

Supporting NASA technical reports

  • NASA NTRS 20210011385 — BASS-II report
  • NASA NTRS 20090012334 — pressure and self-extinguishment
  • NASA NTRS 20240002981 — Saffire VI; evidence outside indexed PSI tables
  • NASA/TM-2008-215260 — Table 1: 1 g versus microgravity flammability limits
  • Olson and Ferkul — Martian-gravity drop-tower study; outside PSI (NTRS 20130010991)

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

OpenAI and Anthropic assistants supported literature exploration, comparative research, brainstorming and refinement of the concept, coding, debugging, documentation and this submission. AI-assisted extraction produced source-quoted claims. OpenAI gpt-6-luna generated candidate answers; automated citation and content checks can replace generated prose with cited records.

Ask EMBER accepts users’ own research questions and runs a live, server-backed evidence review. OpenAI gpt-6-luna generates source-grounded explanations from retrieved NASA records and reports; automated citation and content checks can withhold generated prose and return cited evidence instead. Saved example answers are also available for offline exploration, alongside the live question-answering workflow. The backend supports google/gemini-embedding-2 and google/gemini-decision-1 through OpenRouter for semantic retrieval and decision support, with OpenAI synthesis. Applicability rules and numerical comparisons remain deterministic. The team remains responsible for reviewing generated code, data transformations and explanations.
